cfdna-chromatin-xai · fetal-fraction module (seqFF++)

The Math Behind Every Step

From cfDNA coverage → fetal-fraction SHAP → cell-of-origin
PCA → linear regression closed-form linear SHAP tissue enrichment null model PC ↔ tissue decomposition

Every formula is taken verbatim from extract_ff_shap.R, ff_tissue_proportion.py, pc_tissue_map.R and the plot scripts. Figures rendered on the synthetic 73-tissue demo model.

Overview

Three questions, three stages

The tool is a feature-agnostic explainer wrapped around a fetal-fraction (FF) predictor. It answers three questions in sequence, each feeding the next:

1 · Importance

Which genomic bins drive the FF prediction, and in which direction?

→ SHAP, closed-form

2 · Explanation

What cell types are those bins open in?

→ tissue enrichment vs null

3 · Mechanism

Which latent PCs build each FF direction, and what tissue does each look like?

→ PC ↔ tissue decomposition

$$\underbrace{\text{coverage } x_{i,b}}_{\text{input}}\;\xrightarrow{\text{PCA}\to\text{lm}}\;\underbrace{\hat{FF}_i}_{\text{prediction}}\;\xrightarrow{\text{SHAP}}\;\underbrace{w_b,\;\phi_{i,b}}_{\text{importance}}\;\xrightarrow{\text{atlas}}\;\underbrace{\text{cell of origin}}_{\text{explanation}}$$

The XAI layer reads only the model's bin_loadings and beta — no patient-level data ever leaves the instance.

1Input & feature

The feature: normalized coverage residual

Input

Whole-genome cfDNA sequencing, binned into 50 kb windows on hg19 autosomes (~52 k bins).

Feature $x_{i,b}$

GC- and depth-corrected coverage residual for sample $i$, bin $b$ — not raw counts.

$$x_{i,b} = \text{coverage}_{i,b} - \mathbb{E}[\text{coverage}\mid \text{GC}_b,\,\text{mappability}_b]$$

Concept. Raw coverage is confounded by GC bias and sequencing depth. The model input is the residual after regressing those out, so a non-zero $x_{i,b}$ means "more/less cfDNA landed here than GC predicts" — a biological signal, not a technical one.

Interpretation. Positive residual = bin over-represented (relatively protected / less fragmented); negative = under-represented (open chromatin fragments more → fewer intact fragments → lower coverage). This inversion is central: open chromatin ⇒ low coverage.

2The model

Why PCA first, then linear regression

~52 k bins ≫ number of training samples. Regressing FF on bins directly is rank-deficient and overfits. PCA compresses the bins into ~100 orthogonal components first; the regression runs on those.

$$\text{score}_k(i) = \sum_b L[b,k]\,(x_{i,b}-\bar{x}_b) \qquad \hat{FF}_i = b_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{100} \beta_k\,\text{score}_k(i)$$

$L[b,k]$ — loadings

bin × PC matrix. Column $k$ is a genome-wide spatial pattern (a "meta-bin").

$\beta_k$ — coefficients

how strongly PC $k$ moves FF. Sign matters: $\beta_k$ can raise or lower FF.

Key property. Both maps are linear, so they collapse exactly into one linear model in bin space — no information lost, no approximation. That collapse (next slide) is what makes SHAP closed-form.

3Collapse

Effective per-bin weight $w_b$

Substituting the score into $\hat{FF}$ and swapping the order of summation:

$$\hat{FF}_i = b_0 + \sum_b \Big(\underbrace{\sum_k L[b,k]\,\beta_k}_{\textstyle w_b}\Big)(x_{i,b}-\bar x_b), \qquad \boxed{\,w_b = \sum_k L[b,k]\,\beta_k\,}$$

Input

$L$ (bin×PC), $\beta$ (PC vector). Model object only.

Output

One signed number $w_b$ per bin = the bin's net effect on FF.

Interpretation (verbatim from the code):

  • $w_b>0$ more coverage/openness ⇒ higher predicted FF → fetal / placental-leaning
  • $w_b<0$ more coverage/openness ⇒ lower predicted FF → maternal-leaning

This is a matrix–vector product $w = L\beta$. It needs nothing but the trained model — which is why the whole importance track is computable without any patient data.

4Importance

SHAP is closed-form here

For a linear model the exact Shapley value of feature $b$ for sample $i$ is the weight times the centered feature — no sampling, no KernelExplainer:

$$\phi_{i,b} = w_b\,(x_{i,b}-\bar x_b), \qquad \sum_b \phi_{i,b} = \hat{FF}_i - b_0 \;\;(\text{local accuracy})$$

Aggregated across samples, the tool emits two per-bin tracks:

$$\text{mean\_abs\_shap}_b = |w_b|\cdot\overline{|x_{i,b}-\bar x_b|} \qquad \text{signed\_shap}_b = w_b\cdot\underbrace{\overline{|x_{i,b}-\bar x_b|}}_{\text{mad}_b\,\ge\,0}$$

The sign identity. Because $\text{mad}_b\ge 0$, it can never flip the sign: $\operatorname{sign}(\text{signed\_shap}_b)\equiv\operatorname{sign}(w_b)$. The signed track is anchored to the model weight, independent of any patient.

Model-only track

no coverage matrix → importance $=|w_b|$. Ranking = ranking by |weight|.

Exact-SHAP track

with the training matrix → magnitude $=|w_b|\cdot\text{mad}_b$ (weight × coverage variability). Direction unchanged.

4Importance · figure

Reading the coverage / SHAP track

x-axis

Genomic region — one bin per tick, in chromosome order.

y-axes

top: normalized coverage $x_{i,b}$ (input). bottom: SHAP value $\phi_{i,b}$ (signed contribution to $\hat{FF}_i$).

Interpretation. The local explanation for one prediction. A tall positive SHAP bar pushed this sample's FF up; a deep negative bar pushed it down. Aligning the panels shows why: a bin gets large $|\phi|$ only when its coverage deviates from the mean and it carries a non-trivial weight $w_b$.

5Partition

FF-up vs FF-down bin sets

The signed track partitions every bin by the sign of its weight, then takes the top-$N$ most extreme in each direction (defaults $N\in\{500,1000,2000,5000\}$):

$$\mathcal{U}_N=\text{top-}N\{b: w_b>0\}\ (\text{FF-up})\qquad \mathcal{D}_N=\text{top-}N\{b: w_b<0\}\ (\text{FF-down})$$

Why "FF-up / FF-down", not "positive / negative SHAP"?

NameAnchored toAmbiguous?
positive/negative SHAParithmetic sign — but aggregate or per-sample $\phi_{i,b}$?yes — per-sample $\phi$ flips for patients below the bin mean
FF-up / FF-down$\operatorname{sign}(w_b)$ — sample-independent model weightno — names the biological direction

Same bins, but "FF-up" states what the sign means for the output and sidesteps the per-sample sign-flip. That is the name the downstream analysis uses.

6Explanation

Cell-of-origin: enrichment vs a matched null

For each top-$N$ set, average each tissue's specificity over just those bins, then z-score against random genome:

$$\text{spec\_obs}_t=\frac1N\!\!\sum_{b\in\text{top-}N}\!\!SP[b,t]\qquad \text{spec\_z}_t=\frac{\text{spec\_obs}_t-\mu^{\text{null}}_t}{\sigma^{\text{null}}_t}$$

Null: draw $N$ random bins, recompute the mean, repeat $n_{perm}$ times (default 2000) → $\mu^{null}_t,\sigma^{null}_t$. Two-sided empirical $p$ = fraction of null draws at least as extreme.

$\text{spec\_z}_t$

how many SD more tissue-$t$-specific-open the SHAP bins are than random genome. Calibrated significance.

share$_t$

$[\text{spec\_obs}_t]_+ / \sum_t[\text{spec\_obs}_t]_+$ — positive specificities normalized to sum to 1 = composition.

Interpretation. spec_z answers "is tissue $t$ significant?"; share answers "how big is $t$'s slice?" The null stops "these bins are just open everywhere" from masquerading as a real signal.

6Explanation · figure

Tissue track — grouped bars (default)

Panel A

x: tissue · y: spec_z (vs null) · bars = four top-$N$ cutoffs. "Is this tissue significant?"

Panel B

x: tissue · y: tissue-of-origin share. "How big is its slice?"

Placenta dominant in both panels = the fetal-signal confirmation for the FF-up bins.

6Explanation · new layout

Lollipop layout (--style lollipop, new in v0.6.2)

Axes (flipped)

y: tissue, top-K by $|\text{spec\_z}|$, labels always horizontal. x: spec_z (A) / share (B).

Dots

one colored dot per top-$N$ cutoff (stem from 0). The near-zero tail is dropped with a "+N more near zero" note.

Why it was added. At 73 tissues the vertical bar labels shrink to ~7 pt. The lollipop keeps names horizontal and, by showing the dots across cutoffs, reveals whether a tissue's enrichment is stable as the bin set widens — a robustness read the bars don't give.

7Contrast · new figure

POS-vs-NEG dumbbell (plot_ff_tissue_dumbbell.py, new in v0.6.2)

$$\text{contrast}_t = \text{spec\_z}^{\text{(FF-up)}}_t - \text{spec\_z}^{\text{(FF-down)}}_t$$

Axes

y: tissue (top-K by contrast). x: spec_z. Two dots per tissue: FF-up set FF-down set, joined by a line.

Line length

= the contrast — how strongly that tissue distinguishes fetal from maternal bins.

Reads only the two ff_tissue_results.csv files (POS and NEG) — no recomputation, no atlas reload.

8Mechanism

PC ↔ tissue: β-oriented alignment

The tissue track treats the model as weight-per-bin. But $w_b=\sum_k L[b,k]\beta_k$ — the weights are built from PCs. This stage decomposes the model one layer down. First, how much does each PC's loading pattern resemble each tissue's openness — oriented by the sign of $\beta$:

$$\text{align}_{k,t} = \operatorname{corr}\big(L[\cdot,k],\,\text{openness}_t\big)\times \operatorname{sign}(\beta_k)$$

Why the $\operatorname{sign}(\beta_k)$ factor? Raw correlation says only "does PC $k$ look like tissue $t$?" — direction-agnostic. Multiplying by $\operatorname{sign}(\beta_k)$ rotates it onto the FF axis:

  • red the FF-raising direction of PC $k$ resembles tissue $t$
  • blue the FF-raising direction anti-resembles $t$ (i.e. $t$-openness lowers FF)

Without the flip, a $\beta_k<0$ PC that correlates +0.5 with placenta would look "placenta-positive" while actually lowering FF. After the flip, red consistently means FF-up across the whole matrix — which is the only reason the colorbar can carry one honest "FF-up →" arrow.

8Mechanism

PC ↔ tissue: exact contribution to each direction

Because $w_b=\sum_k L[b,k]\beta_k$ is an identity, each term is PC $k$'s exact additive share of that bin's weight. Averaging over the FF-up / FF-down bin sets:

$$\text{Contrib}_{b,k}=L[b,k]\,\beta_k \qquad \text{pos\_contrib}_k=\frac{1}{|\mathcal U_N|}\!\!\sum_{b\in\mathcal U_N}\!\!\text{Contrib}_{b,k},\quad \text{neg\_contrib}_k=\frac{1}{|\mathcal D_N|}\!\!\sum_{b\in\mathcal D_N}\!\!\text{Contrib}_{b,k}$$

Input

$L$, $\beta$, and the FF-up/FF-down bin sets from Step 5. Model object only.

Output

per PC: pos_contrib, neg_contrib (and their shares of the set's total $|w|$).

Exactness. The per-PC bars for a bin set sum to that set's mean weight — nothing left over. So the figure answers "of the total FF-up signal, how much is built by PC3 vs PC7 vs …?" with an exact decomposition, not an approximation.

8Mechanism · figure

Reading the PC ↔ tissue plot

Panel A — heatmap

y: PCs (labeled PC · best_tissue). x: tissue. color = colorbar: β-oriented alignment; red = FF-up.

Panel B — bars

y: same PCs. x: mean contribution $L[b,k]\beta_k$. FF-up vs FF-down.

Combined reading. "PC3 aligns red with placenta (A) and has a long FF-up bar (B)" → PC3 is the fetal axis. "PC7 aligns blue with monocyte and has a long FF-down bar" → maternal axis. The two panels together give one mechanistic sentence per component.

Cell color vs colorbar

One encoding, shown two ways

Cell color

the value itself — one β-oriented alignment number per (PC, tissue) square, painted on RdBu_r.

Colorbar

the legend that decodes it. Not data — the ruler. Its ticks give magnitude (symmetric, white = 0); its label "FF-up →" gives the sign's meaning.

To decode any cell: match its shade against the colorbar → the ticks tell you the number, the "FF-up →" arrow tells you the direction. Red-and-dark = strongly FF-up-aligned; blue-and-dark = strongly FF-down-aligned; pale = near zero.

The label can say "FF-up →" only because the value is already $\times\operatorname{sign}(\beta_k)$-oriented — otherwise red would mean "positive correlation" and couldn't be tied to a fixed FF direction.

The SHAP figure explains the model's numbers; the tissue figures translate them into biology; the PC figure opens the box to the latent components — with a null model and β-orientation keeping every step honest.

$$w_b=\sum_k L[b,k]\beta_k \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{sign}(\text{SHAP}_b)=\operatorname{sign}(w_b)=\text{FF direction} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{cell of origin}$$
